brief: US 10-year Treasury yields have risen 100bp in 2026 while global equities are up about 13%, a combination that under the Gordon Growth model (value = D/(r-g)) should compress equity valuations as r rises. It hasn't, because g has risen too: Morgan Stanley teams see median S&P 500 EPS growth in the mid-teens, around 20% 2026 EPS growth in Europe, and a net 21-point earnings-beat skew plus 11-point upgrade skew across Asia/EM, so the S&P 500 earnings-yield-to-Treasury-yield gap (MS's preferred ERP measure) is broadly unchanged, which the note reads as a classic mid-cycle, earnings-driven market rather than multiple expansion. The reallocation channel shows no evidence either: ETF flows stay positive and positively correlated across stocks and bonds, the opposite of what reallocation would produce. Companies still prefer debt over equity financing (record IG issuance, hyperscaler bond sales) despite near-6% IG yields, which MS reads as issuers signaling debt is the cheaper option. Caveat: since 1998 the earnings-yield/bond-yield gap explains only about 10% of 12-month stock-vs-bond returns but about half over three years, so near-term resilience does not resolve the longer risk. MS has raised its own yield forecasts on a more hawkish Fed view, raising the bar for earnings to keep outrunning higher rates. The note closes with a preview of the coming week's US and global data calendar.
